# **What is it?** 

The MASS\_SOAR\_Pipeline (Mass At Stellar Separations Pipeline)  is a program that converts multiple contrast curves from magnitudes into individual masses for the primary star and the secondary companion. This pipeline is built specifically for SOAR (Southern Astrophysical Research Telescope) observations, where our data reduction process has contrast measurements at 0.1 and 0.15 arcseconds. 	  

# ***How to use***

## **Input data:** 

The MASS\_SOAR\_Pipeline takes in CSV files. The CSV file must contain this  information: 

- The minimum separation between the two objects, when the magnitude difference between them is zero. This must be in arcseconds. It will accept both apparent and absolute magnitudes.   
- The magnitude difference between the two objects at 0.1 and 0.15 arcseconds and their errors. The code will accept either V-band or I-band magnitudes.    
- The parallaxes and their errors. The code will accept them in arcseconds or in milliarcseconds.   
- The combined magnitude of both objects and the error of the combined magnitudes. The code will accept this in either V-band or I-band. It will accept both apparent and absolute magnitudes. 

## **How to run:**

To run the file, you have to edit the information in the first Jupyter cell:

- Set **csvFile** equal to a string with the directory of your CSV file   
- Set **final\_csv\_name** equal to a string with the name you’d like to use for the output file. Make sure that the name ends with ‘.csv’   
- Set **rhomin** equal to a string with the column name that contains minimum separations.   
- Set **dm1** equal to to a string with the column name that contains magnitude differences at 0.1 arcseconds   
- Set **dm1\_err** equal to to a string with the column name that contains the error on the magnitude differences at 0.1 arcseconds   
- Set **dm015** equal to to a string with the column name that contains the magnitude differences  at 0.15 arcseconds   
- Set **dm015\_err** equal to to a string with the column name that contains the error on the magnitude differences  at 0.15 arcseconds   
- Set **plx** equal to a string with the column name that contains parallax in arcseconds   
- Set **plx\_err** equal to to a string with the column name that contains the error on parallax in arcseconds   
- Set **cMag** equal to a string with the column name that contains the combined magnitudes of both objects in either V-band or I-band  
- Set **colormap** equal to a string with the name of the colormap you’d like to use for the plots.   
- Set **cMag\_err** equal to a string with the column name that contains the error of the combined magnitudes of both objects in either V-band or I-band.   
- Set **cMag\_VBand** equal to *True* if your combined magnitudes are in V-band. Set it to *False* if your magnitudes are in I-band. Note that the code will assume that your combined magnitudes and their errors are in the same band.   
- Set **dm\_VBand**  equal to *True* if your magnitude differences are in V-band. Set it to *False* if your magnitudes are in I-band. Note that the code will assume that your magnitude differences and their errors are in the same band.   
- Set **cMag\_Abs** equal to *True* if your combined magnitudes are absolute magnitudes. Set it to *False* if they’re apparent magnitudes. Note that the code will assume that the combined magnitudes and their errors are the same type of magnitude.  
- Set **dm\_Abs** equal to *True* if your magnitude differences are absolute magnitudes. Set it to *False* if they’re apparent magnitudes. Note that the code will assume that the combined magnitudes and their errors are the same type of magnitude.  
- Set **plx\_arcsec** equal to True if your parallaxes are in arcseconds. Set it to *False* if your parallaxes are in milliseconds. Note that the code will assume that your parallaxes and their errors use the same units.   
- Set **remove\_bad\_points** equal to true if you’d like the code to remove impossible data or data that doesn’t fit within the range of the equations being used. \[See [cell 4](#cell-4:) for details\] 

## **Output Data:** 

The MASS pipeline  will save a new file with the file name you chose for **final\_csv\_name**. The new file will have added several new columns and edited others:

- The **parallax** columns and its errors will have been converted into arcseconds if they weren’t already.   
- A **“Dist (PC)”** and **“err\_dist”** column will have been added. They contain the distances of the objects in PC and their errors, calculated using the parallax data.  
- The **cMag, dm1,** and **dm015** columns will have been converted into absolute magnitude in the V-band if they weren’t already.   
- Columns **Mv1\_015, Mv2\_015**, **Mv1\_015\_err,** and **Mv2\_015\_err** will have been added which contain the absolute V-band magnitudes, and their errors, for the primary star and secondary companion  at 0.15 arcseconds of separation, calculated using the combined magnitude equation \[See [Equations](#equations) for details\]   
- Columns **Mv1\_1, Mv2\_1**, **Mv1\_1\_err,** and **Mv2\_1\_err** will have been added which contain the absolute V-band magnitudes, and their errors, for the primary star and secondary companion at 0.1 arcseconds of separation, calculated using the combined magnitude equation \[See [Equations](#equations) for details\].   
- Columns **Mv1\_rhomin, Mv2\_rhomin**, **Mv1\_rhomin\_err,** and **Mv2\_rhomin\_err** will have been added which contain the absolute V-band magnitudes, and their errors, for the primary star and secondary companion at the minimum separation, calculated using the combined magnitude equation \[See [Equations](#equations) for details\]  
- Columns **M1\_015, M2\_015**, **M1\_015\_err,** and **M2\_015\_err** will have been added which contain the masses, and their errors, for the primary star and secondary companion at 0.15 arcseconds of separation, calculated using the mass-luminosity relationship equation \[See [Equations](#equations) for details\]  
- Columns **M1\_1, M2\_1**, **M1\_1\_err,** and **M2\_1\_err** will have been added which contain the masses of the masses, and their errors, for the the primary star and secondary companion at 0.1 arcseconds of separation, calculated using the mass-luminosity relationship equation \[See [Equations](#equations) for details\].   
- Columns **M1\_rhomin, M2\_rhomin**, **M1\_rhomin\_err,** and **M2\_rhomin\_err** will have been added which contain the masses, and their errors, for the the primary star and secondary companion at the minimum separation, calculated using the mass-luminosity relationship equation \[See [Equations](#equations) for details\].

# **What does the code do?**

## **Cell 1:** 

This cell set gathers information about the input cvs file \[See [how to run](#how-to-run:) for more information\]. 

## **Cell 2:**

This cell contains the important functions that will be called later in the \[pipeline\]. 

- **getIndMags** takes in a magnitude difference and a combined magnitude and their errors. It uses the combined magnitude equation to return the magnitude of the primary and secondary companion, and their errors. \[See [Combined Magnitude Equation](#combined-magnitude-equation:) for details\]   
- **getAbsMag** takes in an apparent magnitude, its distance, and their errors. It uses the absolute magnitude conversion to return the absolute magnitude and the error. \[See [Absolute Magnitude Equation](#absolute-magnitude-equation:) for details\]   
- **getVBand** takes in an I-band magnitude and its error, and converts them into V-band magnitudes. This is done through a linear relationship between the two bands. \[See [I to V-Band Conversion](#i-to-v-band-conversion:) for details\]   
- **getMass** takes a magnitude and its error and converts them into masses using the Mass-Luminosity relationship. \[See [Mass-Luminosity Relationship](#mass-luminosity-relation:) for details\] 

## **Cell 3:**

This cell converts the data into the correct units. 

- The first section reads in the data file   
- The second section converts the necessary columns into numeric values   
- The third section converts the parallax and its error into arcseconds if they weren’t already. Using the parallaxes, it calculates distance and its error.   
- The fourth section converts the combined magnitudes, the magnitude differences, and their errors into V-band if they aren’t already.   
- The fifth section converts the combined magnitudes, the magnitude differences, and their errors into absolute magnitudes if they aren’t already.   
- The sixth section finds the individual magnitudes of the primary and secondary companion for the magnitudes at the minimum separation and the separations at 0.1 and 0.15 arcseconds.   
- The seventh cell finds the masses and errors of each star at each separation. 

## **Cell 4:**  {#cell-4:}

This cell removes impossible data and data that doesn’t fit within the relations we’re using. 

- The first and second sections remove columns with negative magnitude differences at 0.15 or 0.1 arcseconds.    
- The third section removes columns with a minimum separation that’s too high.  
- The fourth section removes columns that have magnitudes that aren’t covered by the Mass-Luminosity Relation. \[See [Equations](#equations) for details\]

## **Cells 5-11:** 

These cells plot the original contrast curves, the individual contrast curves, and the mass plots. The final cell saves the dataframe as a csv.

# **Equations**

## **Combined Magnitude Equation:** {#combined-magnitude-equation:}

$$
m_1= 2.5 \log_{10}\left(1+10^{-0.4\Delta \text{mag}}\right)+cMag 
$$

$$
{\delta m}_{1}=\ \sqrt{(\frac{{(10}^{-0.4\Delta mag})\delta \Delta mag}{1+{10}^{-0.4\Delta mag}}{)}^{2}+\delta cMa{g}^{2}}
$$

$$ 
{m}_{2}={m}_{1}+\Delta mag 
$$  

$$
\delta {m}_{2}=\sqrt{(\frac{\delta \Delta mag}{1+{10}^{-0.4\Delta mag}}{)}^{2}+\delta cMa{g}^{2}}
$$

## **Absolute Magnitude Equation:**  {#absolute-magnitude-equation:}

$$
M = m - 5\log_{10}(d) + 5
$$  
$$
\delta M\ =\ \sqrt{\delta {m}^{2}+(\frac{5*\delta d}{d*lo{g}_{10}(10)}{)}^{2}}
$$

## **I to V-band Conversion:**  {#i-to-v-band-conversion:}

This is a linear conversion between V and I-band, found using linear curve fitting between the V and I-band magnitudes of single stars.

$$
V = C_{0} \cdot M + C_{1}
$$

Where $C_{0} = 1.342419195727928$ and $C_{1}=-0.6388236738633501$

## **Mass-Luminosity Relation:**  {#mass-luminosity-relation:}

This equation is the mass luminosity relationship found in “[The Solar Neighborhood. XXXVII](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.3847/0004-6256/152/5/141)” by G.F. Benedict et al.   

$$
M={C}_{0}+{C}_{1}(V-{x}_{0})+{C}_{2}(V-{x}_{0}{)}^{2}+{C}_{3}(V-{x}_{0}{)}^{3}+{C}_{4}(V-{x}_{0}{)}^{4}
$$

$$
{\delta M}_{}=({C}_{1}+2{\cdot C}_{2}(V-{x}_{0})+{3\cdot C}_{3}(V-{x}_{0}{)}^{2}+{4\cdot C}_{4}(V-{x}_{0}{)}^{3})*\delta V
$$

Where $C_{0}=0.19226$, $C_{1}=-0.050737$,  $C_{2}=0.0101377$,  $C_{3}=\ -0.00075399$, $C_{4}=\ -1.9858e-05$, and $x_{0}=13.0$
